Bacterial_Leaf_Spot.quote: On older plants, infections occur primarily on older leaves and appear as water-soaked areas.
Symptoms on immature fruit are at first slightly sunken and surrounded by a water-soaked halo, which soon disappears.

Bacterial_Speck_Of_Tomato.quote: Bacterial speck produces small (1/16 in.) slightly-raised black 'speck-like' lesions on the developing fruit
On tomato leaves, similar lesions to bacterial spot appear except that faint yellow halos surround the lesions and the leaf may show substantial curling.

Early_Blight.quote: Initially, small dark spots form on older foliage near the ground. Leaf spots are round, brown and can grow up to 1/2 inch in diameter.
Stem infections on older plants are oval to irregular, dry brown areas with dark brown concentric rings.
Fruit spots are leathery and black, with raised concentric ridges. They generally occur near the stem.

Gray_Mold.quote: Gray mold appears on young plants as gray-brown velvety mold covering stems or leaves.
Green fruit decays and turns light brown or gray, starting at the point where it touches other infected plant parts.

Late_Blight.quote: Leaf symptoms of late blight first appear as small, water-soaked areas that rapidly enlarge to form purple-brown, oily-appearing blotches.
Entire leaves die and infections quickly spread to petioles and young stems.
Infected fruit turn brown but remain firm unless infected by secondary decay organisms; symptoms usually begin on the shoulders of the fruit because spores land on fruit from above.

Leaf_Mold.quote: Disease symptoms appear first on the lower leaves of tomato plants.

Leaf_Mosaic_Virus.quote: Leaves show green mottling and may be curled, stunted, and slightly deformed.
Plants may be stunted and are generally somewhat yellowed.

Phytophthora_Blight.quote: Phytophthora blight, caused by the oomycete Phytophthora capsici, causes a root, crown and fruit rot of cucurbits, tomato, pepper, and eggplant.
Phytophthora blight often appears first in low or flooded parts of a field as systemic wilting of the plant.
It is sometimes accompanied by a shriveling of the crown, and fruits may develop soft spots, then 'melt.'

Powdery_Mildew.quote: Symptoms include white superficial mycelium on leaves and stems, yellowing, desiccation, necrosis and defoliation.

Septoria_Leaf_Blotch.quote: Symptoms are evident in the foliage, particularly older (lower) leaves.

Southern_Blight.quote: Often a white mat of mycelium is observed at the base of the stem at the soil line
Eventually the whole plant wilts and fails to recover.

Tomato_Spotted_Wilt_Virus.quote: Plants infected with Tomato spotted wilt virus exhibit bronzing of the upper sides of young leaves, which later develop distinct, necrotic spots.
On ripe fruit chlorotic spots and blotches appear, often with concentric rings.
If tomato and pepper plants are infected early in the growing season, the plant can wilt and die, starting from the top and continuing to the bottom of the plant.

Verticillium_Wilt.quote: Older leaves on tomato plants infected with Verticillium appear as yellow, V-shaped areas that narrow from the margin.
A light tan discoloration develops in the vascular tissue, especially near the base of the plant.
